While the recent controversy surrounding Medha Roopam Case, largely captured media attention towards familial connections of Justice SC Sharma. There is another side which hasn’t gotten as much attention truly required compared to the former raised point, that is “Master of Roster”. This problem is uniquely visible in India out of all democracies who follow the system of dividing their Supreme or Constitutional courts into panel like Germany. But many Supreme or Constitutional Courts around the world to avoid the problem of “Master of Roster” sit en banc, like SCOTUS. It is also one of the points that I believe needs immediate reforms to clamp down arbitrariness in decision making in SC, the Master of Roster gives CJI near dictatorial or at worst unusually concentrated power to single-handedly decide outcome of cases, assuming of course he knows the biases of every Judge and Judge doesn’t get swayed and produces a ruling which doesn’t align with his previous patterns. I am today going to start with history of how CJI gained such power, before that who decided bench composition, abuse of this power and finally solutions from existing system in other democratic countries and a conclusion. Also I would be later putting a master list article outlining which reforms are urgently needed in Supreme Court, and as I write in detail in future, I am going to hyperlink from that list.
History Before Constitution Well to find out where the master of roster power of CJI originated, I had to go through a lot of academic papers, most of them were paywalled, I also found a paper written by Amit Kumar on ResearchGate1 and another wonderful paper written by A Kundu, U Jhunjhunwala in NLUJ law review.2 So in England there was a court called Court of Chancery in medieval times it originated in 14th and 15th centuries as an administrative and judicial body headed by the Lord Chancellor3 and existed till 1875, upon which it was merged into the newly formed High Court by Judicature Acts of 1873–1875.4 In this court there was a clerical position known as Master of the Rolls.12 Later an entire department was established under Master of the Rolls.12 In 17th century, gradually over time Court of Chancery became independent of King and due to this transformation Master of the Rolls got huge powers and was entrusted with the ultimate power of deciding the court’s roster and other administrative duties.12 Now England abolished this system quickly after realising that the power had become centralised in one position or person, Now Master of the Rolls is just the President of the Civil Division of the Court of Appeal of England and Wales and Head of Civil Justice and second in seniority in England and Wales only to the Lord Chief Justice.12 I nearly believed this claim after all it was published in peer reviewed NLUJ law review journal, but it is in fact wrong, I found no indications upon reading the cited sources by the paper that said Master of the Rolls controlled seal of the king, or was his secretary or even controlled roster, Also roster in modern sense wouldn’t have existed back then. Also upon looking at cited sources I came to the realization that NLUJ law review authors may have confused two roles, The role of lord chancellor and master of the rolls who was a clerk under Lord Chancellor and Lord Chancellor controlled the docket of Court of Chancery as Court of Chancery was effectively a one judge court till 19th century presided over solely by Lord Chancellor.56
Infact colonial administrators in India created the position of master of roster as understood in modern sense, Section 200 of GOI Act, 1935 established the Federal Court and Section 214(3) explicitly inserted “Subject to the provisions of any rules of court, the Chief Justice of India shall determine what judges are to constitute any division of the court and what judges are to sit for any purpose.” 1
On June 6, 1949, Dr Bhimrao Ambedkar would go on record in Constitutional assembly debates and say “I may also point out that the provisions contained in article 121 are the same as the provisions contained in article 214 of the Government of India Act, 1935 relating to the Federal Court and article 224 relating to the High Courts. Therefore, there is really no departure from the position as it exists today.” 7 Another member on the same day in CAD, Bakshi Tek Chand will say “Now, Sir, these all are matters which ought to be solely within the jurisdiction of the Chief Justice and the judges of the Supreme Court and there is no reason why they should be subject to approval of the President. If you see the constitution of the High Courts, as they have functioned in the country for the last eighty years or more and also the provisions of the Government of India Acts of 1915 and 1935 relating to these matters, you will find that it is purely within the jurisdiction of the Chief Justice and the judges of the High Court to frame rules in such matters, as the admission of advocates, attorneys, etc. and the constitution of Benches.” 8 This clearly shows that Constituent Assembly believed that administrative power and master of roster will lie with the Chief Justice of the court.
After Constitution Till now it had not become a severe problem because Federal Court in colonial times used to sit en banc in 1940s and 1930s (an assumption because Federal court had 3 judges and did not divide itself into panels) but after subsequent increase in number of judges in 1950s starting from 8 judges SC adopted panel system of two or three judges in a single panel, it became difficult to sit en banc.1910 For 1950s I couldn’t find any accurate source but it can be safely assumed that CJI was master of roster by convention because looking at composition of bench and its biases and the fact that the Chief Justice has been about 6.5 times less likely to be in dissent than other judges on constitution benches since independence.9 K. Subba Rao, he dissented 48 times as a judge, more than any other judge up to that point, but never after becoming Chief Justice. During his tenure the Court as a whole gave more anti-government decisions than at any earlier point, because most likely K. Subba Rao formed benches composed of like minded Judge.911 So it can be presumed from this that in 1950s CJI was indeed master of roster.9 But it was well established by law that Chief Justice of High courts were the master of the roster through several constitutional cases and orders dating back from 1949 till 1990s, I have listed a few:
Rajasthan High Court Ordinance, 1949, para 44, and the 1952 High Court Rules (Rules 54, 55, 73) State v. Devi Dayal, AIR 1959 Allahabad 421 Niranjan Singh v. State, AIR 1974 Rajasthan 171 State of Maharashtra v. Narayan Shamrao Puranik, AIR 1982 SC 1198 Mayavaram Financial Corporation v. Registrar of Chits (1991), Madras HC Inder Mani v. Matheshwari Prasad, (1996) 6 SCC 587 Sohan Lal Baid v. State of West Bengal, AIR 1990 Calcutta 168 but again all these relate to Chief Justices of High Courts only. Also I took a look at Supreme Court Rules, 1966 and found out these lines from Order VII
“Subject to the other provisions of these rules every cause, appeal or matter shall be heard by a Bench consisting of not less than two Judges nominated by the Chief Justice” 12
This tells us, despite constitutional silence and no statutory law or judicial precedent, Chief Justice was Master of Roster, since at least 1966, according to rules of SC.12
State Of Rajasthan vs Prakash Chand & Ors In 1998 we get our first defining judgement, State Of Rajasthan vs Prakash Chand & Ors. Now I will divide the State Of Rajasthan vs Prakash Chand & Ors into facts and holdings sub section to make readers understand easily. We need to remember this specific judgement because it would become very important later on in establishing judicially that CJI is indeed the master of roster and formalising the convention that has continued since pre independence era.
Facts A PIL in the Rajasthan High Court at Jodhpur (W.P. 2949/1996) sought accommodation and benefits for the High Court judges. An intervenor also challenged the constitution of the High Court’s Jaipur bench. Justice B.J. Shethna heard it as a single judge.13
The roster changed, so Shethna J. was required to sit in a Division Bench from 4 September 1997. The State then applied to refer the petition to a Division Bench because it raised constitutional questions.13
Chief Justice Mukul Gopal Mukherjee sent it to a Division Bench, which dismissed it as infructuous on 10 September.13
Meanwhile Shethna J. kept trying to list “part-heard” cases before himself on a separate board. The Chief Justice’s order of 3 September said that providing the roster is the Chief Justice’s prerogative.13
While hearing an unrelated criminal revision (Prakash Chand’s, a conviction under Section 304A IPC), Shethna J. called for the disposed-of writ petition’s record. He made scathing comments about the Chief Justice and the Division Bench, and issued a show-cause notice for criminal contempt against the Chief Justice. He also accused former Chief Justices, including CJI J.S. Verma, of illegally drawing daily allowance and misappropriating public funds.13
Holding The Supreme Court allowed the State’s appeal. It quashed the contempt notice and expunged all of Shethna J.’s comments, held that he had no authority to call for the record, and found his remarks on daily allowance to be factually and legally wrong. It also listed 14 conclusions, including that the Chief Justice is master of the roster, that puisne judges cannot pick and choose cases, and that the Chief Justice can refer even a part-heard case to a larger bench.13
Supreme Court Rules, 2013 Now Supreme Court Rules, 2013 were officially published in Gazette of India on May 29, 2014.14 The Order VI explicitly says,
“Subject to the other provisions of these rules every cause, appeal or matter shall be heard by a Bench consisting of not less than two Judges nominated by the Chief Justice” 14
“Where in the course of the hearing of any cause, appeal or other proceeding, the Bench considers that the matter should be dealt with by a larger Bench, it shall refer the matter to the Chief Justice, who shall thereupon constitute such a Bench for the hearing of it.” 14
Now this will lead to first CJAR (2018) and then CJAR would lead to Shanti Bhushan v. Supreme Court of India.
Shanti Bhushan v. Supreme Court of India Facts Senior advocate Shanti Bhushan, a former Law Minister, filed under Article 32, represented by Dushyant Dave with Prashant Bhushan. He asked the Court to read “Chief Justice of India” in the Supreme Court Rules, 2013 as a collegium of the five senior-most judges. He also asked that the Registry consult senior judges when listing, that listing follow the Rules and not “picking and choosing” benches, and that on urgent mentions only a date be fixed, with the bench set by the Rules. His concern was that the CJI could assign sensitive cases to chosen judges to get a predetermined outcome. Attorney General K.K. Venugopal replied that daily bench allocation by a collegium would be unworkable and cause chaos.15
Holding Sikri J. said the position is undisputed and traced it through Prakash Chand (1998), the Constitution Bench in Campaign for Judicial Accountability and Reforms (2018), which applied Prakash Chand to the Supreme Court, and the three-judge decision in Asok Pande (11 April 2018).15
He accepted that the Constitution is silent on the point and that the position rests on convention that is now engrafted in the Rules. He cited Section 214(3) of the 1935 Act and Order VI Rule 1 of the 2013 Rules, which have the CJI nominate the judges for every bench.15
The Judges’ cases were tied to Article 124 and judicial appointments, so their logic did not extend to roster work, which is daily and administrative.15
The Court said the CJI should act by consultation, with regard to judges’ abilities and specialisation, and that listing must follow the 2013 Rules and the Handbook.15
Campaign for Judicial Accountability and Reforms (2018) As I told earlier to keep State of Rajasthan v. Prakash Chand in mind, as it will play a large role here.
Facts In September 2017, the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) registered an FIR (RC. 10(A)/2017-AC.III) against individuals including I.M. Quddusi (a retired Odisha High Court judge) and representatives of the Prasad Education Trust. The FIR alleged a criminal conspiracy to use illegal gratification to secure favourable judicial orders for de-recognised medical colleges. The underlying medical college matter had previously been heard by a Supreme Court bench headed by Chief Justice Dipak Misra.16
CJAR filed a writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution alleging high-level judicial corruption and seeking an independent Special Investigation Team (SIT) headed by a retired CJI to investigate the matter. A nearly identical petition was filed by advocate Kamini Jaiswal (Kamini Jaiswal v. Union of India, W.P. (Crl.) No. 176 of 2017).16
On November 8, 2017, CJAR mentioned its petition before Court No. 2, presided over by Justice J. Chelameswar (the second senior-most judge) and Justice S. Abdul Nazeer, who issued notice and listed it for November 10.16
On November 9, 2017, the companion petition by Kamini Jaiswal was mentioned before the same two-judge bench (Chelameswar and Nazeer, JJ.), which passed an order directing that the matter be placed before a Constitution Bench comprising the five senior-most judges of the Supreme Court.16
On the morning of November 10, 2017, CJAR’s petition was listed before a two-judge bench of Justices A.K. Sikri and Ashok Bhushan. Noting the November 9 order, that bench directed the matter to be placed before the Chief Justice of India for appropriate orders regarding listing.16
On the afternoon of November 10, 2017, CJI Dipak Misra constituted a five-judge Constitution Bench (which did not include Justice Chelameswar or the next three senior-most collegium judges).16
Holding The Constitution Bench held that the Chief Justice of India alone holds the administrative authority to constitute benches and assign judicial rosters. The Court extended the principles in State of Rajasthan v. Prakash Chand (1998) 1 SCC 1 from High Court Chief Justices directly to the Supreme Court.16
On the judicial side, the CJI is equal to every other judge of the Supreme Court. However, on the administrative side, the CJI possesses singular primacy over the Court’s roster.16
No two-judge or three-judge bench has the jurisdiction to allocate matters to themselves, mandate bench compositions, or direct the CJI to list a case before a specific panel.16
The Court held that any order by another bench directing the listing of a matter before a specific set of judges was non est, ineffective in law, and not binding on the CJI. Bypassing the CJI’s roster authority was held to risk “utter confusion” and institutional chaos.16
Abuses Four Judges’ Press Conference This was the most prolific case of CJI abusing his master of roster power that led to a huge fallout and first of its kind in Indian legal history. On January 12, 2018, the four senior-most judges of the Supreme Court: Justices J. Chelameswar, Ranjan Gogoi, Madan B. Lokur, and Kurian Joseph, held an unprecedented public press conference at Chelameswar’s residence.17
The immediate trigger was the allocation of public interest litigation (PIL) petitions seeking an independent investigation into the mysterious death of Special CBI Judge B.H. Loya (who was presiding over the Sohrabuddin Sheikh encounter case). Despite being an exceptionally sensitive matter, it was assigned to Court 10, headed by a relatively junior judge, Justice Arun Mishra.17
We all know how this event went, CJI Misra would exclude all four judges who spoke against him from the seven important cases to be heard by constitution benches in coming week as decided on roster on January 16.18
Later Asok Pande would bring a petition which stated “unfettered power was being exercised by the Chief Justices in the matter of formation of benches” and called for reforms in master of roster system. A bench consisting of Misra, Khanwilkar and Chandrachud rejected the petition on 11 April. Later Chandrachud will write “the Chief Justice of India is first among equals and has the authority to decide allocation of cases and setting up of benches.” 19
The abuse could be seen with naked eye from a mile away, and this manifestly arbitrary abuse led to first demands for reforms albeit suppressed by the very same Court and Judge it was advocating against. In an ideal system Dipak Misra should have recused from the case regarding deciding power of roster but he did not do so, that again points to another weak point in our judicial system that is there exists no mandatory recusal policy unlike in other countries who have strict statutory guidelines for recusal and potentially annulment of judgement on appeal if conflict of interest is discovered like US.
Other abuses in 2023 In late 2023, several senior members of the Supreme Court Bar Association, including Senior Advocates Dushyant Dave and Prashant Bhushan, submitted formal open letters to CJI D.Y. Chandrachud raising alarms over systemic listing irregularities. Numerous politically charged matters such as bail pleas of activists booked under UAPA (including Umar Khalid and Bhima Koregaon accused) and petitions by opposition political figures were repeatedly shifted away from benches that had already heard substantive arguments. Instead, they were reassigned to a specific bench headed by a junior judge (Justice Bela M. Trivedi), in direct contravention of the Supreme Court’s published listing conventions, which prescribe that part heard matters remain before the senior judge. Then out of the blue, a long-pending contempt plea concerning the central government’s delay in notifying judicial appointments was suddenly deleted from the cause list of Court 2 (presided over by the second-senior-most judge, Justice Sanjay Kishan Kaul). To which Justice Kaul directly replied on record “I am sure that the Chief Justice must be aware of it… I have not deleted the matter or expressed unwillingness to take it. Some things are better left unsaid.” 2021
Medha Roopam Case Now this directly brings us back to 2026, to the Medha Roopam case. Now we need to first understand the fact that who is Medha Roopam and what she did. Medha Roopam is a UP cadre IAS officer, whose father is current CEC Gyanesh Kumar (in hot waters for arguably more severe matter). Now Medha Roopam invoked NSA against Delhi University student activist Akriti Chaudhary following a labor protest in Noida (labor protest itself occurred in April 2026 and Akriti herself had been arrested earlier on protest site.) on the recommendation of police in May 2026.22 On September 2, 2026 a division Bench comprising Justice Atul Sreedharan and Justice Achal Sachdev quashed the detention order after nearly five months of custody on the fact that DM acted without application of mind to “make an example” and court awarded ₹5 lakh in compensation to Chaudhary, ordering the sum to be recovered from the personal salaries of Medha Roopam and other responsible police personnel, alongside adverse entries in their service books.22 But Medha Roopam and her lawyer immediately appealed to SC and on Sept 23, 2026 a Supreme Court bench presided over by Justice Satish Chandra Sharma and Justice N. Kotiswar Singh stayed the operation of the High Court’s directions concerning the ₹5 lakh salary deduction and judicial strictures against the officers pending regular hearing.23 It was later clarified that the High Court’s quashing of the NSA detention was not stayed by the interim order.24
Now this was the basic timeline of events, but a concern arises and first raised was that Justice SC Sharma’s son is in ECI standing counsel as an advocate in Madhya Pradesh HC and his other son is also in MP government panel as an advocate.25 Now again I talked about this in last article regarding the two judge bench decision on ECI Act of Parliament and how it got referred to a higher bench and how personalities like Saurav Das and Prashant Bhushan immediately began accusing Justice SC sharma of being biased and spreading rumor that he has been guaranteed a post retirement seat by Government.26 I discussed it at length to defend the decision (it was constitutional) and point out the problems with the argument presented and even took a deep dive into history where such condition existed but the government still lost.26 But I mentioned in that article that I would write separately about Medha Roopam case as it was irregular.26 Now again I would not go onto Justice SC Sharma familial connections as those points as I said in previous article may appear significant but are worthless except the recusal and disclosure one.26
What I want to focus on is the role of CJI Suryakant and how he subverted the roster and gave the case to junior judges instead of the senior one who should have heard it in the first place. This is a classic textbook case of Judicial deference in face of a roaring executive. If we go and access the official roster list of SC, we would find that matters related to habeas corpus and preventive detention have been assigned to CJI Suryakant, Justice Vikram Nath, Justice BV Nagarathna and Justice MM Sundresh only.27 Also not to mention the fact that the accused in this case Akriti, had earlier approached SC and her case was placed before the benches of Justice BV Nagarathna and Justice Ujjal Bhuyan.28 We could also further see that all other habeas corpus cases got correctly listed before the above mentioned first four benches only.28 Only Medha Roopam case got handed to the bench led by Justice SC Sharma.28 Now the roster also says Justice SC Sharma could take on other matters if specifically assigned but for that special matter can only be assigned by CJI who is the master of roster.28 Also not to mention as pointed out during the hearing, after briefly hearing Solicitor General and senior counsel for the State, the Bench muted the audio of the virtual proceedings and closed media access to the video feed for the remainder of the hearing.29 Again this fueled a lot of early speculation about the case and certainly damaged reputation of court.
Now again usually connected matters are listed before the same benches, so we could have logically said that Akriti matter was already once heard by Justice BV Nagarathna bench (even though it was disposed by May 8 with liberty to approach HC)28 and should have been listed before her bench again also other Noida-protest matters are pending before Justice BV Nagarathna,2829 but CJI curiously referred it to a much junior bench and already knowing that the Judge had familial connections with ECI. Also a point to consider from the other side that this is a mere interim order and final outcome has not been pronounced, so we couldn’t say that it is all rigged, maybe the interim pause was only for the judges to dig deeper into the matter. I would say on this point that social media speculators have overblown the familal connection issue over a wide range while ignoring the fact that this is not a final order and merely speculating or using supports of rumors saying that Justice SC Sharma is biased. This is plainly browbeating a judge because he didn’t issue an order that the social media speculators wanted. I have spoken at lenght about this type of browbeating in my previous article.26
Even if we concede the above point to opposition that this is merely an interim order, we still arrive at a case of abuse of roster. It can be probably derived that CJI Kant didn’t want to upset the executive over this matter and chose a path of deference. If we look at the past cases of the aforementioned benches listed for habeas corpus petition, we find that their orders are usually pro rights or pro people, not a shocking discovery. Also we know from past case history that justice BV Nagarathna usually doesn’t shy away from ruling against government in personal liberty matters and Also we have no reason given for why the matter was assigned to this particular bench, this is another huge problem of SC that is institutional opacity which it uses to frame judicial independence, The entire structure of collegium is rested on the fact that Judges selecting Judges through a Institutionally opaque system would somehow guarantee institutional independence. Also opacity is practiced by SC because somehow common people knowing the reason why such a administrative measure was taken would somehow lower institutional independence.
Reforms and Conclusion As I have said, Indian SC is not unique in the aspect of dividing the courts into panel, many other courts also sit panel wise like Supreme Court of UK or Constitutional Court in Germany or ECHR. While many solutions exist, the most favorable I find is that followed by ECHR, I have read ECHR rules of court and German Constitutional Court rules303132 and interpolated it to the Indian context and drew up an abstract of how such reform will look like.
First is an annual allocation plan, and the full court must adopt it unanimously at the starting of each year. The plan will lay down subject categories, standing panels, the rotation schedule and an urgent-matters protocol, and then it would be published to the public. Now second thing we go to is standing panels, the court is divided into panels for a fixed term, Composition is based on Seniority, Origin and Gender as decided in annual allocation plan and adopted by full court unanimously. Third the cases go by subject category, then are assigned among panels by round-robin or random draw, with an audit log this significantly reduces power of CJI under current master of roster system as the cases now get assigned randomly on probability. Fourth each bench is drawn from its panel by a published rotation, with the senior-most judge presiding. Part-heard matters stay with their bench. Fifth, within a bench, the lead judge is chosen under principles set for the year as laid down in annual allocation plan. Disagreements go to the panel. Sixth the most comprehensive one, which lays down how constitutional benches are formed, referral decisions go to a rotating referral panel with six-month terms, not a single bench. Under Article 145(3), at least five judges are needed. The CJI and the next most senior judge sit ex officio, and the remainder are drawn by lot, with balance criteria. The draw is public, with the Registrar present and minutes published. Seventh a binding recusal rule is published and in cases of non disclosure the decision is automatically annulled. Eighth is the oversight part, I am borrowing this one from German Basic Law, which speaks of “lawful judges”. In this system if any deviation occurs and one of the sides thinks the deviation is not correct or believes it to be malafide then the party can flag a breach and try to reverse the decision by arguing that the case was not heard by a “lawful judge”. Also an annual public report on deviations and a route for litigants to flag a breach.
The SC should separately also address their opaque system, while my proposed reforms make many things public, the other parts of SC like the appointment procedure by collegium is too opaque and it must be replaced, I will write about it in detail, some other time. Arguably SC using opacity to defend institutional independence causes more harm to its reputation and standing than it would to its independence if it was an open book. Also other supreme courts like Constitutional Court in Germany or ECHR or Constitutional court in South Africa have stellar judicial reputation and arguably are more shielded from interference and enjoy more judicial independence because they are not opaque, so when a judgement is pronounced nobody can point finger toward the institution and say “it was biased” or “procedure was violated”, unlike in Medha Roopam case where institutional opacity immediately led to finger pointing by Social Media and fueling fire to the wider allegations of conspiracy that were already growing around independent institutions like SC or ECI. I would like to point out that Nepal has also abolished the master of roster system.33 But India being the world’s largest democracy which would arguably requires a more robust and vigilant Judiciary, instead got one filled with opacity. This has led to recent and huge wave of loss of public trust crisis. It is high time that SC does reforms to bring transparency as it cannot afford to lose constitutional legitimacy as an independent court in front of the public eyes in a country where independent institutions are increasingly viewed with mistrust.

title: Master of Roster

content:
Recently, following IndianExpress Report or Expose on ECI, there has been lot of fallout be it political, social or legal or judicial- Wait, judicial? Yes, judiciary has been dragged into this matter by many online commentator, activists and political strongman (even lawyers) related to both government and opposition figures for albeit different reasons. I will primarily be focusing on some remarks by Saurav Das and surprise, Prashant Bhushan (especially targeting Hon’ble Justice SC Sharma).1
Saurav Das Rapid fire of tweets First tweet So First I would be starting with Saurav Das First tweet,2 he said and I will quote:
“This is how the Supreme Court allowed theft of elections in our country. These judges have much to answer, including the location of their spine. It is useless to have such judges who only delay crucial petitions that challenge the rot in our system. The stealing of the young generation’s right to vote for change has been aided, both intentionally and unintentionally by some Supreme Court judges.” 2
First of all it is a great loaded sentence, This was his reponse to a judgement by a two judge SC bench referring the ECI case to a CJI to form a larger Constitutional Bench because Justice Dipankar Datta and Justice SC Sharma arrived at two different conclusions using legal logic.3 The entire argument between the opinion of judges boils down to two main contention point, Justice Dipankar Datta was arguing that this case doesn’t need to be referred to a larger bench because constitutionality of matter has been sufficiently decided in Anoop Baranwal (supra).3 But Justice SC Sharma contends on this point and says that Anoop Baranwal v UOI only made interim provisions till parliament passed an act in 2023, after that the Act of Parliament that is being challenged needs to be challenged on new constitutional grounds and pursuant to Art 145(3) a Constitutional Bench needs to be convened by CJI.3
Apparently this judgement got on nerves of Saurav Das leading to first aforementioned tweet, for to be clear this is the standard administrative process by which a case whether constitutional or any other cases go through and yes this process is slow and yes the process needs to be reformed, infact it needs to be overhauled completely (will write about that a diff time). Saurav Das could have argued about reforms and can have highlighted it but no he buried a legitimate point under conspiratorial framing using words “intentional”, “aided” and “spine” and he also tried to character assassinate the Justices, where he could have raised a really good and legitimate point.
Second Tweet Well we all know what the second tweet is going to be about, he is going to target a judge, isn’t he? Well we all could see from a kilometer away that it would obviously be Justice SC Sharma. But oh boy, get ready for the foul language of second tweet4
“Justice Satish Chandra Sharma must understand that people are not idiots to buy your opinion which has just now led to a delay in deciding the constitutionality of Election Commissioners appointments. Your opinion is invalid.” 4
First of all cool down with the language, Saurav, Honble Justice is holding a constitutional position, I know you could have said the same words in a respectful way but chose to use these words for drama. Second the opinion of Justice SC sharma isn’t egregious at all! Let me get some of his opinion and I am going to quote it word by word:
“In my opinion, the arguments advanced on behalf of the respondents by Mr. Venkataramani, learned Attorney General for India and Mr. Mehta, learned Solicitor General are well-founded. The said Act has been recently enacted pursuant to the decision of the Constitution Bench in Anoop Baranwal v. Union of India here is no authoritative decision of this Court till date pronouncing on the constitutional validity of the said Act. A judicial decision in light of what the Constitution provides has to be given by this Court while it is seized of the issue of vires of Section 7 of the said Act and its other provisions. The decision on these writ petitions would be the first of its kind and it is all the more necessary that a reference is made.” 3
Basically learned Justice is saying that he finds merit in arguments of government counsel and he asserts that court hasn’t pronounced any decision regarding the act itself, Court in Anoop Baranwal (supra) only decided what should be done till parliament has passed an act and parliament did pass an act in 2023, Court did not give any ruling or observations about what the Act should contain or be structured (That would be a violation of Separation of powers if Court passed such orders.) So according to him in order to ascertain whether Section 7 is Ultra Vires or not cannot be decided by this bench because the bench has no legal authority to decide it and a constitutional bench must be made to find if Section 7 is vires or not.
“In this context, the learned Solicitor General relied upon the judgment of a Constitution Bench of this Hon’ble Court in the NJAC case, wherein the Court had held that the presence of even the Law Minister in the Collegium for the selection of Judges of the High Courts and the Supreme Court was violative of the doctrine of separation of powers. Building upon the aforesaid constitutional principle, the submission of the learned Solicitor General was that a corresponding degree of constitutional independence must also be recognized for the Executive as well as the Legislature. He submitted that the Committee constituted under the Rules framed under Article 324 deserves to be declared legal though dominated by the members of the executive. The submission was not as a criticism of the Collegium system or regarding the role of the executive in the appointment of Judges. n my opinion, it was a submission to the effect that if the Constitution Bench has held that the presence of outsiders in the collegium as violative of doctrine of separation of powers, a similar independence should be read in the executive also and the rules framed under Article 324 be not declared void on the ground either that it does not have any outsider in the Committee of selection or there is pre-dominance of only executive in the committee of selection.” 3
Again learned Justice is arguing that just like in NJAC, the Court asserted its authority to be independent from grasp of Executive and Legislature, Similarly Executive and Legislature have right to assert their own independence. Even though I personally find this reasoning for an office like ECI flawed for number of different reasons but constitutionally and legally speaking Justice SC Sharma is right, it is basic separation of powers.
“Having read the decision in Anoop Baranwal (supra), my understanding is that it was dealing with the constitutional vacuum and noticing that no law had been enacted and while leaving it to the Parliament to enact the law, the Constitution Bench proposed an ad hoc arrangement whereby the Hon’ble the Prime Minister, the Hon’ble Chief Justice and the Leader of the Opposition were to form an interim committee to select the Election Commissioners. No doubt, to the extent law has been declared under Article 141 is to be applied but whether or not Parliament was justified in not including a neutral selector in the selection committee is an important question arising for the first time before this Court. Since, it is a substantial question of law as to interpretation of the Constitution, which has not been dealt with in any precedent, the plain language of Article 145(3) read with Order 38 of the Supreme Court Rules does not leave any room for a decision on such question finally by the present combination.” 3
“My view on this contention is this. Old or new, whatever be the character of the statute, if validity of such statute or a part thereof is questioned on valid grounds as failing the constitutional test and if this Court has previously not had the occasion to deal with and pronounce on such grounds, a reference would seem to be in order. This contention of the petitioners militates against the mandatory provisions of Article 145(3) of the Constitution read with Order 38 of the Supreme Court Rules and, hence, has failed to impress me.” 3
“Contention raised that the said Act effectively seeks to legislatively overrule Anoop Baranwal (supra), which is impermissible, is again unmeritorious because of the nature of exercise performed by the Constitution Bench. Had it not been an interim arrangement, the consequence could have been otherwise.” 3
“The submission that reference to a Constitution Bench would permit the respondents to launch a challenge to the decision in Anoop Baranwal (supra) and reopen issues settled by it, short-circuiting the reference procedure and, thus, misusing the provisions of Article 145(3) of the Constitution, proceeds on a misapprehension. Fair and free elections being a part of the basic structure has been acknowledged in the precedents relied on and no Court can or would, possibly, doubt it now. But whether the said Act fails the test of free and fair elections has to be independently examined.” 3
Again nothing novel has been said by the Justice in these points, He is basically arguing Anoop Baranwal only proposed an interim arrangement for choosing ECI until parliament passed an Act. After now the Act has been passed the challenge to validity of the Act must now occurs on the ground of that such said Act violates Basic structure of constitution (Free and Fair elections) and a Constitutional Bench must be established to test the validity. Nothing wrong or legally egregious with the opinion of Justice SC Sharma. But this got Saurav Das to react because apparently the case didn’t went the way he wanted and wanted the Justice to rule on his opinion rather than law and wrote “Your opinion is invalid”,4 Even though Justice SC Sharma reached a opposing view that of Justice Dipankar Datta, his reasoning has followed or is grounded in “procedural propriety”, he followed the mandatory referral logic of Article 145(3), but that doesn’t make his opinion any less legally valid, ultimately it is a legal opinion rested on well founded pillars of Constituion and Statutory law.
Third Tweet Now we arrive at the third tweet, maybe we can wonder and think, Saurav Das wrote something grounded on material in this tweet, but alas no, we instead get a veiled threat masquerading as “accountability”
“We need to open up the files on judges’ appointments. Who are these judges we have no clue. Why are they calling apple an orange? We have no clue. Why are they seeing gross illegality as legal? We have NO IDEA. Open the judges’ files now. Let us see those appointment papers!” 5
Ok regarding “Who are these judges we have no clue” so you can read all about biodata and career of a SC judge on Supreme Court website as it is public opinion and they are not calling “Apple Oranges” they are calling “Apple Apple”. Secondly, I myself am a huge critic of the current collegium system regarding various points and issues I will write on length regarding my issues in a separate article and instead I support a system of appointment to SC akin to how British Judges are appointed to British Supreme Court, but we need to look at the context in which Das made this demand — he is illegitimately deploying it here as a punitive response to a judge writing a legally grounded opinion he disagreed with, rather than as part of a general institutional reform position.
Case of Prashant Bhushan Now going away from Saurav Das drama, we address Prashant Bhushan, Senior advocate in SC. For the last few days he has been focused two cases “The ECI case” and the “Noida DM case”, both of which share one judge in common. You guessed it, Honble Justice SC Sharma. Now I would not be arguing about merits of “Noida DM case” as I too believe that in this particular case procedural powers has been abused and the case does not has a final Judgement till now and all I can do is speculation. Instead I would be focusing on the ECI case and Prashant Bhushan insistence on that Justice SC Sharma is biased towards government. Prashant Bhushan has claimed as far as he has heard a rumor that Justice SC Sharma has been offered post of “chairman of the National Company Appelate Tribunal” and this rumor is apparently rife in “bar corridors”.6 This is an unsubstantiated accusation, because he has quoted a tweet from Saurav Das7 accusing or more likely implying a quid pro quo between Justice SC Sharma and government, regarding a wide range of factors, I am going to go one by one through them and point out historical and legal judgements that same conditions existed in past but still Judges ruled independently. Also the specific tweet7 has a second part about Noida DM case which I am not going to cover because I have mentioned earlier, this case is irregular and I am anyways going to address that in detail in an upcoming article.
First tweet by Prashant Bhushan We start with this:
“The Madhya Pradesh High Court’s website records that Justice Sharma’s son, who enrolled in 2017, is the standing counsel for the Election Commission of India. He is also the standing counsel for the Central Board of Direct Taxes and the Income Tax Department. His younger son, enrolled in 2020, is also the standing counsel for the MP Public Service Commission. Should he not have recused from hearing the ECI case & also Gyanesh Kumar’s daughter’s case?” 8
with an attached livelaw article.9 So the premise is Justice SC Sharma’s son is allegedly involved with 4 different government posting10 also allegedly empanelled as counsel for the ECI.9 So the question is being asked that “Could under such circumstances Justice SC Sharma have ruled independently?”, The answer to this question lies in history and precendent, which I will lay out one by one.
History Let us take Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer, he before serving as Supreme Court judge was Minister of Home Affairs of Kerala under CPI government in 5 April 1957 – 31 July 1959.11 In Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain, 1975, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi sought an urgent, absolute stay from the Supreme Court against the Allahabad High Court judgment that disqualified her, to get full context, the CPI was in coalition with Congress at this period of time and would also go on to support imposition of emergency in 1975 initially.12 And guess who was heading the vacation bench to which Indira Gandhi appealed, Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer, now he could have easily granted the stay and left Indira Govt intact, but did he do it? No, Justice Krishna Iyer (sitting as vacation judge) rejected the government’s demand for an unconditional stay, granting only a conditional stay that barred her from voting in Parliament.
Justice K.S. Hegde in Kesavananda Bharati v UOI voted to create the Basic Structure Doctrine, striking down the government’s attempt to assert unfettered power over constitutional amendments, this would cost him his Chief Justiceship leading to his immediate resignation. He was formerly a member of the ruling Congress party and a Rajya Sabha MP (1952–1957) before being elevated to the judiciary. He after resigning would go on to become 7th speaker of Lok Sabha under Janata Government.13
You see and observe these example and you might ask why we didn’t get biased judgement? Well Justices of Supreme Court being Constitutional Judges are bound by an oath which has words “I will duly and faithfully and to the best of my ability, knowledge and judgment perform the duties of my office without fear or favour, affection or ill-will”.14 Now I know, there have been many corrupt Judges who have no respect for the Oath, but according to all public information available, it has been the exception, rather than trend, Justices usually abide by the oath.
Arguably Krishna Iyer and Hegde had a closer reason to issue favor to government due to their own immediate political past. We are alleging in this specific case that Justice SC sharma colluded because his adult’s son’s client, the gymnastics and circumstantial evidence needed to even scratch this claim speak for themselves.
Now the main point I am bringing all these historical examples and the oath and the trends is to invoke a basic assertion “Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence” by Carl Sagan,15 as much applicable it is in astronomy or any other science field, it is as much as applicable in this case. Both Mr Prashant Bhushan and Saurav Das are making an extraordinary claim67 and they must provide us extraordinary evidences, not rumors or circumstantial evidences and screenshots connecting strings with each other and then giving a theory to explain all that. These unfounded snippets about alleged corruptions, do us no help except feeding fuel to a already going fire about credibility of SC and fueling more fire by browbeating judges. So in future they do not give adversarial judgements against public opinion of the time. To the point of Justices doing mental gymnastics and putting their own words in amendments and laws passed by a democratic parliament even if legally there is no trouble or malice or doubt and the law is clear, but only because there exists a public pressure which is supported by a majority. As much as Judiciary needs to be shielded from Executive and Legislature, it needs to be also shielded from exceptional public pressure carried by a majority, whose opinion would result in erosion of constituiton and democracy itself, but there exists no such insulation from public pressure in India, allowing significant public figures to browbeat judges into submission and thereby eroding the constitution and laws that they themselves claim to protect.
Legally In India there is no law or binding rule of mandatory or automatic recusal, arguably this is the largest blindspot in Indian Judiciary, so I will concede this point. The only statute applies to lawyers that is BCI rule 6,16 Judges usually follow the recommended but not binding RESTATEMENT OF VALUES OF JUDICIAL LIFE adopted by SC in 7th May, 1997,17 it is basically a recommendation. We will refer to clause 4 and clause 7 specifically
Clause 4:
“A Judge should not permit any member of his immediate family , such as spouse, son, daughter, son- in-law or daughter-in-law or any other close relative, if a member of the Bar, to appear before him or even be associated in any manner with a cause to be dealt with by him.” 17
This literally says that if a Judge has a family member practicing law, then such family member cannot appear before the related Judge in any case, BCI rule 6 also state the same thing for the lawyer side but it has statutory teeth.
Clause 7:
“A Judge shall not hear and decide a matter in which a member of his family, a close relation or a friend is concerned.” 17
Now here things get a little spicy, we can go down two paths from here regarding the interpretation of word “concerned”. But still this is not binding but entirely left to conscience of the sitting judge. Indian law treats recusal as an ethical/discretionary norm for the judge himself rather than a hard legal duty.
I concede this point to attack a more flawed point put up by LiveLaw and Prashant Bhushan.89 First let us take Manak Lal v. Dr. Prem Chand (1957)18 established the “reasonable apprehension of bias” basically meaning “had appeared for a party in it, or had a personal/pecuniary interest in its outcome.” I would argue Here, the son isn’t appearing in either case; he holds a standing government-panel empanelment that’s structurally unrelated to whether the ECI Act 2023 is struck down or upheld. A ruling against the Act doesn’t cost the ECI its standing counsel, doesn’t affect the son’s fees, and doesn’t touch his professional standing — the case is about the composition of the selection committee, not about any ECI litigation his son might be handling.
Second I will argue, Standing counsel positions (his elder son also holds panels for CBDT, Income Tax, and his younger son for MP PSC)10 are fixed-term government appointments, not success-fee or per-case arrangements tied to how any single case comes out. The argument by Prashant Bhushan and quoted LiveLaw article “his son’s growth depends on the ECI winning” 89 doesn’t make a lot of sense, losing a constitutional challenge to an appointment law doesn’t threaten the empanelment itself.
Third, the Jaya Thakur case3 is about the validity of a statute Parliament passed after Anoop Baranwal, ECI itself was more of a bystander of this law than a real party pressing its own institutional interest. This attacks and weakens the “judge is deciding a case that benefits the entity his son serves” 89 claim by Prashant Bhushan and quoted LiveLaw article.
Fourth, There is no legal requirement for Justice SC Sharma to recuse, as pointed above there is no Indian Supreme Court ruling holding that a judge must recuse merely because an adult child, in independent practice, holds a government panel brief for an entity that happens to be a beneficiary (not even a principal party) in a constitutional case before the judge.
But again I will state that there is no mandate for judges to be recused, it all depends on conscience of the justices. This truly needs to be mended, by either a law of parliament or binding regulations by SC. Even though I pointed 4 serious flaws with the arguments presented, I will use the phrase “justice should not only be done, but must also be seen to be done”, justice might have been done (I personally believe the decision to refer the case to constitutional bench is good, because it would prevent future malicious litigation by a hurt executive) and is legally correct, but the “seen” part the most essential part was not fulfilled. I also want to be clear that this is a real structural failure, the absence of a binding recusal rule is a legitimate object of criticism regardless of who raises it or why, and it doesn’t become less true because Bhushan happens to have raised it for all the wrong reasons. Bhushan doesn’t stop at ’the system doesn’t guarantee the appearance of impartiality’ premise. He goes further, using that gap to assert an actual quid pro quo and a promised post-retirement post, without offering any substantial evidence for either and instead relying on rumors and gossip. The structural criticism is fair; the leap to personal corruption is not.
Second Tweet by Prashant Bhushan Second tweet is
“The more important question is: Has the govt promised to give him a critical & plum post retirement job? The bar corridors are rife with rumours that he is slated to be made the chairman of the National Company Appelate Tribunal, a post which is vacant today.” 6
Again as I have pointed many times in this article, this is simply accusation of quid pro quo based on rumors and circumstantial evidence without having any cold hard proof. Again we are posing a rumor that could have been started for any number of reason as far as we know. What I am asking for that if Saurav Das and Prashant Bhushan have some hard evidence then they must bring it in front of court or public instead of relying on unwarranted rumors. Now they may argue for contempt of court or investigations against judges is difficult, I concede this point, investigation against constitutional judges is indeed very difficult and opaque process but that doesn’t mean we should instead rely on rumors and stoke a fire which can turn out to be wrong later. Also not including the fact that Prashant Bhushan has a habit of accusing CJIs and Justices of corruption in past without any proof and has earned a contempt of court hearing many times himself. Without such evidence this is browbeating judge to rule on majority opinion of a the populace instead of ruling on basis of statutory law and constitution.
Conclusion The main conclusion from this entire saga is people need to stop speculating and relying on rumors to justify their goals because a constitutional case in which they had their own political interests didn’t go their way as they wanted. Instead of challenging it through the proper appellate channel, they immediately started posting unwarranted claims on social media that cannot be publicly verified. Other lesson learned by judiciary and government is to communicate their information to public correctly instead of being silent when others accuse you. Special lesson for judiciary as a whole is to do structural reforms and stop the opacity regarding roster management, compulsory or mandatory or automatic recusal guideline framed by Supreme Court or enshrined in law by Parliament. Most important lesson is stop “BrowBeating” just because case didn’t go the expected way we wanted, doesn’t mean we should browbeat the judge using public majority opinion into submission. A judge must rule on basis of law and constitution rather than majority opinion of public, these incidents make future judges compliant to rule on majority public opinion rather than on basis of law, leading to risks for judicial independence. As I said judiciary may have secured independence from Executive or Legislature but they have not secured independence from public. There must be a separation of Public opinion (most of the time is legally incorrect) and the Judiciary which is a creature of Constitution and law and must rule on those grounds only. If these Political commentators like Saurav Das want to get their public opinion into law then they must approach the correct institution that is parliament to show their public support and get law passed, instead of appearing in front of unelected judges and demanding those judges to decide cases on basis of majority public opinion and insert their words into the law that was passed by a democratic Parliament which itself draws its power from public.

summary: Recently, following IndianExpress Report or Expose on ECI, there has been lot of fallout be it political, social or legal or judicial- Wait, judicial? Yes, judiciary has been dragged into this matter by many online commentator, activists and political strongman (even lawyers) related to both government and opposition figures for albeit different reasons. I will primarily be focusing on some remarks by Saurav Das and surprise, Prashant Bhushan (especially targeting Hon’ble Justice SC Sharma).1
title: BrowBeating

content: We live in a era of rapid misinformation and post truth content, every lies are spread like wildfires by social media users to every corner of the world. Today I want to focus on a specific type of misinformation that has plagued my field, not since advent of social media, but long long ago, since the advent of media itself, yes! I am talking about law. Multiple times I have seen not only social media but traditional media themselves since long time have potrayed the controversial judgements (actually they are not controversial, I am using that term for the sake of framing only) of court in a twisted way. For example let us take a snippet I recently came across, a news media agency (reputed) had published a headline along the lines “Entering woman’s house, lifting her clothes not rape attempt: Jharkhand HC” now this snippet was shared in a subreddit, I stumbled on, and in comments I saw people who have not read a single line of law or a bare act for that matter commenting ills upon the judge, calling out his caste, and other horrendous comments I cannot describe, but the media agency did not clarify that the judgement was absolutely right! I commented and explained it on that post so I am not going to elaborate but it just boils down to difference between “Preparation” and “Attempt”, Under BNS and other Indian laws, unless explicitly stated Preparation is generally not punishable (there are statutory exception like UAPA), and I read the judgement and facts of this case and the evidences submitted by the Prosecution and all of it pointed that the act this man has committed in this case was not Attempt but rather Preparation which is not punishable by law (BNS criminalises Rape and Attempt to Rape only) then how could the judge under what authority would have punished the person? No one in the comments berating the judge and law had that answer, Should the judge have inserted his own thoughts and words into the law and specifically a penal law passed by a democratically elected parliament to punish this guy? (As a lot of people in comment were saying) NO! Absolutely not! Judge was strictly following law laid down by the act of parliament (This is called Strict Construction, it is a legal doctrine Indian courts use usually in criminal cases). The HC was also following a previous judgement of Supreme Court of India (henceforth referred to as SCI) as laid in Tarkeshwar Sahu vs State of Bihar (Now Jharkhand) on 29 sept, 2006, This is called doctrine of stare decisis which makes judgement pronounced by a Higher court binding on a lower court (Also further adopted explicitly in article 141 of Constitution). The problem is that I had just to do all this research (I knew a lot of doctrine from top of my mind but still had to look up the specific facts of case), that should actually had to be done by the media agency that published the report first! Later in small words towards the end they had included just two sentences, I kid you not but two sentences about “overt proximate act” nothing else! Now you can see the problem, the reporting problem, legacy media and Social media both are the biggest offender of publishing misleading headlines, titles, descriptions, in order to attract TRP and views so that they can gain profit or validation or internet clout. This has effects on judiciary, taking a judge’s judgement or words out of context and then use it to criticise, name call, or harras them or their charecter as a person, has serious effects on their lives, this disempowers them and the entire legal community to give out controversial or challenging judgement that has the capabilty to transform fundamental rights or bring transformative justice, but this type of behaviour from broader community only entices the judge to do deference! Deference towards executive, legislature, society, political strongmans, you name it! This is the reason why I have decided to start this blog, I am not advocating for absolute un criticism towards judiciary, I am advocating for valid on point criticism while calling or pointing out the offenders who are spreading legal mis info and a smear campaign against the institution to lower it’s standing and browbeat the judges, that needs to stop. I will not post much, maybe one article per week, sometimes, Mainly either finding the worst misleading title of week and educating about the truth or Explaining legal doctrine used in Indian Laws so that you can yourself point out the misinfo. Not only Indian laws, I would be discussing, sometimes broadly on topic of Common law and British Legal precedents (mainly historical POV) or US constituional law for a comparative analysis. I would conclude or end this article by saying “What has to be done, needs to be done right now”.

title: A Food for Thought
